page.text: To fully grasp the necessity of this project, it is vital to examine the massive scale and
the current operational state of the Kenyan retail and small business sector. Ofﬁcial
data indicates that there are over 7.4 million Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises
operating in Kenya today. These businesses collectively employ approximately 14.9
million people, which represents a massive portion of the national workforce. The
sector is so signiﬁcant that it contributes approximately 40 percent to the national
Gross Domestic Product. In recent years, these small businesses accounted for an
astonishing 85 percent of all new jobs created in the country.
Despite this massive economic scale, the sector operates in a highly informal
manner. Of the 7.4 million businesses, only about 1.6 million are formally licensed and
registered, leaving a staggering 5.8 million businesses operating entirely in the
informal economy.
In this vast market, mobile money is the undisputed king of payments. Safaricom's
M-Pesa network processes hundreds of billions of dollars annually and is used by
roughly 96 percent of Kenyan adults. It is the default payment method for everything
from large electronics purchases to tiny daily grocery runs. However, this heavy
reliance on mobile money creates a massive administrative burden for business
owners. When a customer pays via M-Pesa, the payment conﬁrmation data lives
securely within the telecommunications company's network, while the operational
data what speciﬁc item was sold, who the cashier was, and how much stock is left
lives in a completely separate cash register, a basic spreadsheet, or a paper notebook.
In addition to these payment tracking challenges, the regulatory environment in
Kenya has recently shifted in a way that directly impacts everyday retail.
